newsitem.title: UK: British Telecom sets sights on global arena.
newsitem.headline: British Telecom sets sights on global arena.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc's announcement on Friday that it is in talks to take over U.S. player MCI Communications Corp confirms its determination to build a global empire.

BT's board will be locked in talks over the weekend to seal a deal with MCI, the second-largest U.S. long-distance carrier, and to restore its reputation as a global force after an embarrassing failure to strike a deal with British rival Cable and Wireless Plc in May.

BT said there were no guarantees of a deal but the stakes are high as the two firms stand on the brink of an estimated $22 billion deal which would propel it into corporate history as the second biggest U.S. takeover ever after the 1989 landmark Kohlberg, Kravis & Roberts buyout of Nabisco for $25 billion.
BT already paid $4.3 billion in 1993 to take a 20 percent in MCI stock, and sources close to the deal said BT is likely to offer cash and stock to acquire the rest of the company.
In 1994 BT and MCI created Concert Communications Co, a $1 billion joint venture to provide global corporate communication services using IT technology.
The spur for BT's international expansion is increasing competition at home which has squeezed prices and a need to develop the international muscle to tackle global rivals.
BT has made significant strides in straddling the world telecoms map but its critics have said its grip on global markets could be tighter.
Already BT has developed alliances in Spain, Germany, Italy, Sweden, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Japan and India.

Its most signifcant international deal so far this year was in September as it took a 25 percent stake in Cegetel, a French telecoms consortium led by Compagnie Generale des Eaux for 1.1 billion pounds ($1.8 billion) and the share capital of BT France.
Also, this year BT has commitments to invest around one billion pounds ($1.6 billion) in a joint mobile phone venture with German utilities group Viag AG.
It also took a 25 percent stake in Clear Communications, New Zealand's second biggest telecoms company and set up a joint venture with Microsoft to market computer networking and on-line services.
But despite these successes, the collapse of merger talks with C&W put BT under renewed pressure to tie up with another major international partner.
A deal with C&W would have created the world's fifth biggest telecoms group in revenue terms but financial and regulatory hurdles wrecked the plans.
Hard on the heels of the C&W debacle came a blow from Germany last month as RWE AG pulled out of an alliance with BT and Viag AG and, to add insult to injury, opted to link up with C&W instead.
But BT's chairman Sir Iain Vallance vowed earlier this year, that the group, whose net debt gearing has fallen to an almost unheard-of 7.4 percent, would look at "radical opportunities" to expand.
BT made 869 million pounds ($1.39 billion) in the first quarter of the current financial year and is on course to ring up three billion pounds ($4.8 billion) in profits in 1996.
With a market capitalisation in excess of 22 billion pounds ($35.2 billion), it ranks in the top five of British companies.
BT's privatisation in 1984 marked the start of the transformation of the British telecommunications market from a state-run monopoly into a fast-moving, competitive sector where BT leads the pack.

But after a golden decade of commercial expansion and domestic profitability, it has been pulled into an ever-tighter straitjacket by government regulators who have accused BT of anti-competitive practices and further liberalised the market.

In June, Britain opened up the international telecommunications market to all carriers. At the same time BT has to fight off competition from dozens of cable television firms who are offering telephone and entertainment services.
Last year BT claimed to have 93 percent of the British residential market for phone calls and to derive over half of its 13.9 billion pound ($22.24 billion) turnover from Britain.
In total it has operations in 30 countries and employs more than 130,000 people.
